A (Introduction to Fields)

Words: 244 Articles: 7
2012 OurBigBook.com

A1

Words: 244 Articles: 6
A OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 40 Articles: 1
A1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 40
a OurBigBook.com
The degree of a field extension is the dimension of the larger field, regarded as a vector space over the smaller field:
[K:F]=dimF​K.​
(1)
The scalar multiplication is the multiplication of K restricted to scalars in F. A finite extension has finite dimension; otherwise the degree is infinite.

b

Words: 109 Articles: 1
A1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 109
b OurBigBook.com
The notation K=F(δ) means that K is the smallest subfield containing both F and δ, namely the simple field extension generated by δ. Its elements can be expressed as rational functions in δ with coefficients in F and nonzero denominator.
Write d=δ2∈F. The element δ is a root of X2−d, so its minimal polynomial over F has degree at most two. Since δ∈/F, that degree cannot be one. The degree of the simple field extension equals the degree of the minimal polynomial, giving
[F(δ):F]=2.​
(2)
In particular 1,δ form an F-basis, so every element is uniquely a+bδ. This argument also works in characteristic two; separability is not needed for this part.

c

Words: 95 Articles: 1
A1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 95
c OurBigBook.com
Choose α∈K∖F. Since [K:F]=2, the linearly independent elements 1,α form a basis of K over F. Thus there are a,b∈F with α2=a+bα. The assumption on the characteristic of a field allows division by two. Set
δ=α−2b​.
(3)
Completing the square gives
δ2=a+4b2​∈F.​
(4)
Also δ∈/F, since otherwise α=δ+b/2 would lie in F. Because α∈F(δ) and δ∈F(α), these generated subfields agree. The basis representation shows F(α)=K, hence
K=F(δ),δ2∈F.​
(5)
The square-root generator is obtained by translating an arbitrary generator to remove the linear term of its quadratic relation.

a

Words: 56 Articles: 1
B1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 56
a OurBigBook.com
A left group action of G on a set S is a map G×S→S, written (g,s)↦g⋅s, satisfying
e⋅s=s,(gh)⋅s=g⋅(h⋅s)​
(6)
for every s∈S and g,h∈G, where e is the identity element of G. In particular each g acts by a bijection, whose inverse is the action of g−1.

b

Words: 76 Articles: 1
B1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 76
b OurBigBook.com
Given a group action, define ρ(g)(j)=g⋅j. Each ρ(g) is a permutation, since ρ(g−1) is its inverse. The action law gives, for every j,
ρ(gh)(j)=(gh)⋅j=g⋅(h⋅j)=(ρ(g)ρ(h))(j).
(7)
Thus ρ:G→Sn​ is a group homomorphism​.
Conversely, given a group homomorphism ρ:G→Sn​, put g⋅j=ρ(g)(j). Since a homomorphism sends the identity to the identity permutation, e⋅j=j. Also
(gh)⋅j=ρ(gh)(j)=ρ(g)(ρ(h)(j))=g⋅(h⋅j).
(8)
These are exactly the two group action axioms, so the construction defines the required action.

c

Words: 105 Articles: 1
B1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 105
c OurBigBook.com
The three nonzero vectors in F22​ are e1​, e2​ and e1​+e2​. An invertible linear map permutes this three-element set, so part (b) gives a group homomorphism
ρ:GL2​(F2​)⟶S3​.
(9)
If a matrix acts trivially on all three vectors, it fixes both basis vectors e1​,e2​, so it is the identity matrix. Thus the kernel of a group homomorphism is trivial and ρ is injective.
To count the domain, its first column may be any of the three nonzero vectors. The second column must be outside the two-element span of the first, leaving two choices. Hence
∣GL2​(F2​)∣=3⋅2=6=∣S3​∣.
(10)
An injection between these finite sets of equal size is surjective, proving
GL2​(F2​)≅S3​.​
(11)

a

a OurBigBook.com
For a positive integer n, Euler's totient function counts the integers in a complete residue system that are coprime to n:
φ(n)=#{k:1≤k≤n, gcd(k,n)=1}.​
(12)
For n>1 this is equally the count with 0<k<n. The convention gives φ(1)=1.

b

Words: 63 Articles: 1
C1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 63
b OurBigBook.com
Let Rn​={k∈Z:0<k<n, gcd(k,n)=1}. The map k↦n−k sends Rn​ to itself because
gcd(n,n−k)=gcd(n,k)=1.
(13)
Applying it twice returns k, so it is a bijection. Reindexing the finite sum by this bijection gives
k∈Rn​∑​k=k∈Rn​∑​(n−k).​
(14)
There is no need to assume that every residue belongs to a pair of distinct elements; the reindexing also handles the fixed point when n=2.

c

Words: 43 Articles: 1
C1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 43
c OurBigBook.com
Write S=∑k∈Rn​​k. Adding the two equal sums from part (b), and using ∣Rn​∣=φ(n), gives
2S=∑k∈Rn​​{k+(n−k)}=∑k∈Rn​​n=nφ(n).
(15)
Therefore
S=21​nφ(n).​
(16)
Equivalently, the average of the positive reduced residues is n/2, a consequence of their symmetry under reflection about that midpoint.

d

Words: 34 Articles: 1
C1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 34
d OurBigBook.com
The positive integers below 30 coprime to 30 are
1,7,11,13,17,19,23,29.
(17)
There are eight, so φ(30)=8. Their sum can be grouped into four pairs summing to 30:
1+7+11+13+17+19+23+29=120=21​⋅30⋅8.​
(18)
This agrees with the formula.

D (Integration)

Words: 296 Articles: 4
2012 OurBigBook.com

D1

Words: 184 Articles: 1
D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 184
D1 OurBigBook.com
A sigma-algebra F on Ω contains Ω, is closed under complements relative to Ω, and is closed under countable unions. Consequently it contains the empty set and is closed under countable intersections. A measure space is a triple (Ω,F,μ) with a map μ:F→[0,∞] satisfying μ(∅)=0 and countable additivity on pairwise disjoint measurable sets.
For the increasing sequence, set C1​=A1​ and Cn​=An​∖An−1​ for n≥2. These measurable sets are disjoint, their union is A, and AN​=⋃n=1N​Cn​. Thus countable additivity and finite additivity give
μ(A)=n=1∑∞​μ(Cn​)=N→∞lim​n=1∑N​μ(Cn​)=N→∞lim​μ(AN​).​
(19)
The identity permits the value infinity; it uses no subtraction of infinite measures. This is continuity from below of a measure.
For a decreasing sequence, the analogous assertion is not always true. On Ω=N with the counting measure, take Bn​={n,n+1,…}. Then ⋂n​Bn​=∅, so μ(B)=0, whereas μ(Bn​)=∞ for every n and their limit is infinity.
A sufficient extra condition for continuity from above of a measure is μ(B1​)<∞. Indeed B1​∖Bn​ increases to B1​∖B, and the increasing-sequence result gives
μ(Bn​)=μ(B1​)−μ(B1​∖Bn​)⟶μ(B).
(20)
More generally it suffices that one of the Bn​ has finite measure. The missing finiteness assumption is exactly what the counterexample violates.

D2

Words: 112 Articles: 1
D OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 112
D2 OurBigBook.com
On any bounded parameter interval ∣t∣≤T, the derivative of the integrand has the integrable majorant
​∂t∂​[e−x2cos(2xt2)]​=∣4xte−x2sin(2xt2)∣≤4Txe−x2.
(21)
The dominated convergence theorem therefore justifies differentiation under the integral sign at every real t, giving
f′(t)=−4t∫0∞​xe−x2sin(2xt2)dx.
(22)
Use integration by parts in this absolutely convergent integral, with xe−x2dx=−21​d(e−x2). Both boundary terms vanish, since the sine is zero at x=0 and the Gaussian tends to zero at infinity. Hence
∫0∞​xe−x2sin(2xt2)dx=t2∫0∞​e−x2cos(2xt2)dx=t2f(t).
(23)
It follows that f′=−4t3f, or equivalently (et4f(t))′=0. This identity holds on all of R, including zero. With the supplied Gaussian integral value,
f(t)=2π​​e−t4(t∈R).​
(24)
The fourth power comes from the printed phase 2xt2; the parameter has been differentiated with that phase throughout.

i OurBigBook.com
The map is K-Lipschitz continuous when
dY​(f(x),f(x′))≤KdX​(x,x′)for every x,x′∈X.​
(25)
The same finite Lipschitz constant K must work for all pairs of points.
ii
Words: 41 Articles: 1
a OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 41
ii OurBigBook.com
The map is uniformly continuous when, for every ϵ>0, there is a δ>0 such that
dX​(x,x′)<δ ⟹ dY​(f(x),f(x′))<ϵfor all x,x′∈X.​
(26)
The choice of δ may depend on ϵ but must be independent of the locations of x and x′.

b

Words: 26 Articles: 1
E1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 26
b OurBigBook.com
Given ϵ>0, choose δ=ϵ/K>0. If dX​(x,x′)<δ, the Lipschitz condition yields
dY​(f(x),f(x′))≤KdX​(x,x′)<Kδ=ϵ.
(27)
This single δ works for every pair, proving the map is uniformly continuous:
δ(ϵ)=ϵ/K.​
(28)

c

Words: 59 Articles: 1
E1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 59
c OurBigBook.com
The distance to a set is finite and nonnegative because A is nonempty. For x,x′∈X and every a∈A, the triangle inequality gives
d(x,a)≤d(x,x′)+d(x′,a).
(29)
Taking the infimum over a yields DA​(x)≤d(x,x′)+DA​(x′). Interchanging x and x′ gives the opposite inequality. Together these imply
∣DA​(x)−DA​(x′)∣≤d(x,x′).​
(30)
Thus the distance to a set is 1-Lipschitz continuous. No closedness, compactness or attainment of the infimum was used.

d

Words: 55 Articles: 1
E1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 55
d OurBigBook.com
For fixed x∈X, the function a↦d(x,a) on A is continuous, indeed 1-Lipschitz continuous by the reverse triangle inequality. A continuous real-valued function on a nonempty compact space attains its minimum by the extreme value theorem. Hence some a0​∈A satisfies
d(x,a0​)=a∈Amin​d(x,a)=DA​(x).​
(31)
The metric is symmetric, so this is also d(a0​,x). Compactness supplies attainment of the infimum.

E2

Words: 364 Articles: 8
E OurBigBook.com

a

Words: 49 Articles: 1
E2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 49
a OurBigBook.com
A basis of a topology B is a family of open subsets such that every open set is a union of members of B. Equivalently, for every U∈T and x∈U, some B∈B satisfies
x∈B⊆U.​
(32)
The empty open set is represented by the empty union.

b

Words: 120 Articles: 1
E2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 120
b OurBigBook.com
Define T to be all unions of members of B, including the empty union. Then ∅∈T and the covering assumption gives X∈T. Arbitrary unions of such sets are again unions of basis members.
For two members U=⋃i​Bi​ and V=⋃j​Bj′​, distribute intersection over union:
U∩V=⋃i,j​(Bi​∩Bj′​).
(33)
Each intersection is a union of members of B by the second assumption, so U∩V∈T. Repeating gives closure under all finite intersections. These are precisely the topology axioms. Every B∈B belongs to T, and every set in T is a union of such members by construction. Thus
T={⋃C:C⊆B},B is a basis for T.​
(34)

c

Words: 103 Articles: 1
E2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 103
c OurBigBook.com
The product topology on X×Y has as a basis all open rectangles
U×V,U∈TX​,V∈TY​.​
(35)
Thus a subset W⊆X×Y is open precisely when, around every (x,y)∈W, there are open U∋x and V∋y with U×V⊆W. These rectangles cover the product, and their pairwise intersections are rectangles because (U×V)∩(U′×V′)=(U∩U′)×(V∩V′). Hence they define a topology by part (b).
This is equivalently the coarsest topology making the two coordinate projection maps continuous: the preimages of factor-open sets are the open strips U×Y and X×V, whose finite intersections are the basis rectangles.

d

Words: 92 Articles: 1
E2 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 92
d OurBigBook.com
Let {Bi​:i∈I} and {Cj​:j∈J} be countable bases of the two factors. The family
D={Bi​×Cj​:(i,j)∈I×J}
(36)
is countable, since the Cartesian product of two countable sets is countable. It is a basis of a topology for the product topology: given a product-open neighbourhood of (x,y), choose a contained open rectangle U×V, then basis members with x∈Bi​⊆U and y∈Cj​⊆V. Their product contains (x,y) and is contained in the original neighbourhood. Therefore
The product has a countable basis.​
(37)
In standard terminology, a finite product of second-countable spaces is second-countable.

a

a OurBigBook.com
The function is continuously differentiable when all its first partial derivatives exist on U and are continuous there. Equivalently, h has a Fréchet derivative at every point and the map x↦Dh(x) is continuous. For a scalar-valued function,
Dh(x)v=∑j=1n​∂j​h(x)vj​.
(38)
On the open domain, continuous first partial derivatives ensure that this linear expression is the total derivative.

b

Words: 34 Articles: 1
F1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 34
b OurBigBook.com
For differentiable maps with compatible domains, the multivariable chain rule is
D(h2​∘h1​)(x)=Dh2​(h1​(x))∘Dh1​(x).​
(39)
In Jacobian matrix notation this is matrix multiplication. In particular, if both maps are continuously differentiable, the composition is continuously differentiable. Componentwise,
∂j​(h2​∘h1​)ℓ​(x)=∑r=1m​∂r​(h2​)ℓ​(h1​(x))∂j​(h1​)r​(x).
(40)

c

Words: 63 Articles: 1
F1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 63
c OurBigBook.com
Let L(x,y,z)=(x−y,y−z,z−x). This is a linear map, hence smooth; composing it with the given C1 function proves that g=f∘L is continuously differentiable by the chain rule. Write f1​,f2​,f3​ for the first partial derivatives, evaluated at L(p). Then
gx​=f1​−f3​,gy​=−f1​+f2​,gz​=−f2​+f3​.
(41)
Adding these identities gives
gx​(p)+gy​(p)+gz​(p)=0.​
(42)
Geometrically, L(p+t(1,1,1))=L(p), so g is constant along every line in the diagonal direction; its derivative in that direction must vanish.

d

Words: 109 Articles: 1
F1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 109
d OurBigBook.com
An embedded k-dimensional submanifold M⊆Rn is locally a coordinate k-plane: for every p∈M, there are open neighbourhoods U∋p, V⊆Rn and a diffeomorphism Φ:U→V with
Φ(M∩U)=V∩(Rk×{0}n−k).
(43)
For the present C1 setting, Φ and its inverse are continuously differentiable; in the smooth convention both are smooth.
A tangent vector to M at p is a velocity γ′(0) of a continuously differentiable curve γ:(−ϵ,ϵ)→M with γ(0)=p. The tangent space is the collection of all these vectors:
Tp​M={γ′(0):γ(0)=p, γ is a C1 curve in M}.​
(44)
In the local coordinates above, it is DΦ(p)−1(Rk×{0}n−k), so it is a k-dimensional linear subspace of Rn.

e

Words: 88 Articles: 1
F1 OurBigBook.com
Solution
Words: 88
e OurBigBook.com
The regular level set theorem says that for a C1 map g:U⊆Rn→Rr, if Dg has rank r on g−1(c), then g−1(c) is an (n−r)-dimensional submanifold and
Tp​(g−1(c))=kerDg(p).
(45)
Here r=1 and the given rank condition makes the zero set a two-dimensional submanifold. It is nonempty because g(0)=f(0)=0. Part (c) gives
Dg(p)(1,1,1)=gx​(p)+gy​(p)+gz​(p)=0.
(46)
Consequently
(1,1,1)∈kerDg(p)=Tp​Mfor every p∈M.​
(47)
There is also a direct curve proof: g(p+t(1,1,1))=g(p)=0, so the entire line through p in this direction lies in M. Its velocity at zero is exactly the required tangent vector.

G (Calculus of Variations)

Words: 190 Articles: 2
2012 OurBigBook.com

G1

Words: 190 Articles: 1
G OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 190
G1 OurBigBook.com
For variations vanishing at the endpoints, the Euler-Lagrange equations are
dtd​Fr˙​−Fr​=0,dtd​Fθ˙​−Fθ​=0.​
(48)
Differentiate the stated energy expression using the chain rule. The acceleration terms cancel, leaving
dtdH​​=r˙(dtd​Fr˙​−Fr​)+θ˙(dtd​Fθ˙​−Fθ​)−Ft​.​
(49)
Along a stationary trajectory the two brackets vanish. Thus dH/dt=−Ft​, and in the absence of explicit time dependence H is constant​.
In plane polar coordinates, the squared speed is r˙2+r2θ˙2, so the kinetic energy is T=21​m(r˙2+r2θ˙2). An inverse-square central gravitational force has potential energy proportional to 1/r. With the sign convention printed in this paper, write V=km/r, giving
F=T−V=2m​(r˙2+r2θ˙2)−rkm​.
(50)
For attraction to a star of mass M⋆​, this convention has k=−GM⋆​<0. Keeping k real and signed is essential; no sign is changed in differentiating the printed functional.
Since Fr​=mrθ˙2+km/r2, Fr˙​=mr˙, Fθ​=0 and Fθ˙​=mr2θ˙, the equations of motion are
r¨−rθ˙2=r2k​,dtd​(mr2θ˙)=0.​
(51)
The second equation gives the conserved angular momentum J=mr2θ˙; equivalently rθ¨+2r˙θ˙=0. The autonomous-functional identity gives a second conserved quantity,
H=r˙Fr˙​+θ˙Fθ˙​−F=2m​(r˙2+r2θ˙2)+rkm​=T+V.​
(52)
This is the total mechanical energy; for attractive gravity the potential contribution is negative because k<0.

H (Classical Mechanics)

Words: 152 Articles: 2
2012 OurBigBook.com

H1

Words: 152 Articles: 1
H OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 152
H1 OurBigBook.com
Away from a collision, let r=q1​−q2​ and D=∣r∣>0. The Lagrangian is
L=21​m1​∣q˙​1​∣2+21​m2​∣q˙​2​∣2−V(D).​
(53)
Differentiating D2=r⋅r with respect to x1​ and x2​ gives 2D∂x1​​D=2(x1​−x2​) and 2D∂x2​​D=−2(x1​−x2​). Therefore
∂x1​​D=−∂x2​​D=Dx1​−x2​​.​
(54)
The other coordinates give ∇q1​​D=r/D and ∇q2​​D=−r/D. Substituting these into the Euler-Lagrange equations yields equal and opposite central forces:
m1​q¨​1​=−DV′(D)​r,m2​q¨​2​=DV′(D)​r.​
(55)
Adding the equations shows that the derivative of the total linear momentum is zero, so P=m1​q˙​1​+m2​q˙​2​ is constant. For the total angular momentum, the terms q˙​i​×q˙​i​ vanish, giving
dtd​(m1​q1​×q˙​1​+m2​q2​×q˙​2​)​=q1​×(−DV′​r)+q2​×(DV′​r)=−DV′​(q1​−q2​)×r=0.​
(56)
Thus both stated vectors are conserved quantities.
The total energy is also constant. Define E=21​m1​∣q˙​1​∣2+21​m2​∣q˙​2​∣2+V(D). Since D˙=r⋅(q˙​1​−q˙​2​)/D,
E˙​=m1​q˙​1​⋅q¨​1​+m2​q˙​2​⋅q¨​2​+V′D˙=−DV′​r⋅(q˙​1​−q˙​2​)+V′Dr⋅(q˙​1​−q˙​2​)​=0.​
(57)
Hence E=T+V(D) is conserved​. The explicit cancellation establishes energy conservation for an arbitrary smooth separation-dependent potential, throughout any collision-free trajectory.

The interior time-independent Schrödinger equation for a free particle is
−2mℏ2​(ψxx​+ψyy​)=Eψ.​
(58)
Confinement by the rectangular infinite well imposes Dirichlet boundary conditions: ψ=0 at x=0,b and y=0,5​b. The wave function is square-integrable and may be normalized to unit probability on the rectangle.
Separation of variables gives products of the one-dimensional well states,
ψn,ℓ​(x,y)=51/4b2​sinbnπx​sin5​bℓπy​,n,ℓ=1,2,….
(59)
The Hamiltonian is the sum of the independent x and y kinetic-energy operators, so the one-dimensional energies add. Put C=π2ℏ2/(2mb2). Then
En,ℓ​=C(n2+5ℓ2​).
(60)
For n=1, increasing ℓ gives 6C/5,9C/5,14C/5,21C/5. The smallest energy with n≥2 is also 21C/5, attained at (2,1); all n≥3 give larger energies. Thus the ground and first three distinct excited energy levels are
levelgroundfirst excitedsecond excitedthird excited​E6C/59C/514C/521C/5​(n,ℓ)(1,1)(1,2)(1,3)(1,4),(2,1)​​​
(61)
The largest listed energy therefore has energy-level degeneracy 2​, since the two product eigenfunctions are linearly independent and no other pair solves 5n2+ℓ2=21.

This is Bernoulli's theorem for a steady irrotational flow: irrotationality makes the same constant apply throughout a connected region, rather than only along an individual streamline.

The method of images places a vortex of the opposite circulation at z0​ below the wall, outside the fluid domain. Superposition with the stagnation flow gives

Pr(Xn+1​=j∣Xn​=in​,…,X0​=i0​)=Pr(Xn+1​=j∣Xn​=in​).​

A time-homogeneous chain additionally has transition probabilities independent of n, written Pij​=Pr(Xn+1​=j∣Xn​=i). The displayed single transition matrix in the subsequent parts specifies this time-homogeneous case.

First the entries must be nonnegative: together with the given a,b≥0, validity of the transition matrix requires 0≤a≤1 and 0≤b≤1/3. Every row then sums to one.
The only incoming edge to state 2 is 1→2, of probability a. If a=0, no other state can reach 2, so the chain is not irreducible. If a>0, all edges in the directed cycle
1⟶2⟶3⟶4⟶1
(78)
have positive probability, since P23​=1/3+b>0, P34​=1 and P41​=1/2. Traversing this cycle connects every state to every other state. Therefore
Irreducible exactly when 0<a≤1,0≤b≤31​.​
(79)

Words: 141 Articles: 1

Solution

ii OurBigBook.com
Within the valid parameter rectangle, suppose a>0 and b<1/3. The chain is then irreducible by part (i). State 1 has a two-step return 1→2→1 and a three-step return 1→2→4→1, both of positive probability. Its period of a state in a Markov chain therefore divides both two and three, hence equals one. Irreducibility gives the same period to every state, so the chain is aperiodic.
If b=1/3 and a>0, every transition goes between the two classes {1,3} and {2,4}. Returns must have even length, while 1→2→1 has length two. Thus the irreducible chain has period two.
If a=0, the closed communicating class {1,3,4} alternates between {1,3} and {4}. Its states have period two, using the positive two-step returns through 4. Consequently the chain is not aperiodic, regardless of how the transient state 2 is classified. Combining the cases,
Aperiodic exactly when 0<a≤1,0≤b<31​.​
(80)

A polynomial pn​∈Πn​ is a best polynomial least-squares approximation when it minimizes the weighted error norm over all polynomials of degree at most n:
∥f−pn​∥≤∥f−q∥for every q∈Πn​.​
(110)
Equivalently it minimizes ∫01​x−1/2(f(x)−q(x))2dx. The weight is integrable, so the expression is finite for continuous functions; it defines a genuine norm because a continuous function with zero weighted squared integral must be identically zero.

∥f−q∥2=∥f−pn​∥2+∥pn​−q∥2≥∥f−pn​∥2.
(111)
Taking square roots proves
pn​ is a best least-squares approximation.​
(112)
Equality can hold only when ∥pn​−q∥=0, hence pn​=q, so the best polynomial is unique. Completeness of the ambient space is unnecessary for this orthogonality argument.
